note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Spence Electrical Ltd has a three-year business plan to grow its maintenance contracts. Which document turns this into what the crews will do over the next six months?
options: The company's articles of incorporation
The tool and test equipment inventory
The operational plan for the period
The staff handbook on dress and conduct

questions.stem: Which question does an operational plan answer, rather than the long-term strategic plan?
options: Who does which tasks, with what, and by when?
What should the company look like in ten years?
Which new countries could the company move into?
What are the company's mission and its values?

questions.stem: You are a lead electrician. Which part of the operational plan is usually yours?
options: Setting the company's prices for the whole year
Approving the company's whole annual budget alone
Choosing the company's bank and insurers
Giving input and leading your crew to deliver it

questions.stem: Which objective for a maintenance crew is written in a SMART way?
options: Answer breakdown calls faster than we did before
Reach 90% of breakdown calls within 4 hours by June
Try to be the best maintenance crew in the parish
Improve our customer service as much as possible

questions.stem: Which KPI best measures the quality of a crew's installation work?
options: The number of vans the crew uses each week
The share of jobs passing inspection first time
The number of hours the crew spends on site
The amount of cable the crew buys each month

questions.stem: Why should a KPI have a target and a time period, such as 'callbacks below 3% each quarter'?
options: So the figure can be left out of the reports
So it can be changed whenever results are bad
So that nobody needs to collect any data
So results can be compared and judged

questions.stem: Before the plan is finalised, the manager asks you to consult your crew. What is the most useful thing to ask them?
options: What could stop us meeting these targets, and what would help?
Do you all agree that the targets are fine just as they are now?
Who on the crew should take the blame if targets are missed?
Would you like the plan to be printed in colour this time?

questions.stem: A senior electrician says the plan allows too little time for wiring each house. What should you do?
options: Tell him the plan is fixed now and can never be changed
Ignore him, as he complains about everything
Check his reasons against past job data and report

questions.stem: Which list covers the physical resources an electrical crew needs in the plan?
options: Mission, vision and values
Profits, dividends and taxes

questions.stem: The plan needs 1 120 crew-hours of work next month. Each electrician is available for 160 hours a month. How many electricians are needed?
Next month needs 520 labour hours, but only 440 hours are available. Overtime costs J$1,500 an hour. What will it cost to cover the shortfall with overtime?
Your crew's insulation tester is due for calibration in the middle of a busy month. What is the best plan?
options: Skip the calibration until the busy month is over
Book it early and arrange a calibrated spare
Borrow any tester from a friend's company
Use the tester anyway and fix the results later

questions.stem: The vans keep running out of 20 A breakers in the middle of jobs. Which change to the plan helps most?
options: Set a minimum van stock and a weekly reorder check
Buy a full year's supply of every item at once
Tell the crew to borrow breakers from the client
Let each electrician buy parts with their own money

questions.stem: The materials budget for May was J$250,000 and actual spending was J$230,000. What is the variance?
options: J$230,000 over budget
J$20,000 over budget
J$20,000 under budget
J$480,000 under budget

questions.stem: A job's labour budget was 200 hours and it took 230 hours. By what percentage did labour go over budget?
The price of copper cable rises sharply halfway through the plan period. What should the supervisor do?
options: Keep quiet and hope the budget still balances out
Report the effect on costs and suggest options
Use thinner cable than the design states
Stop all jobs until the prices come down

questions.stem: Which is a fixed cost for an electrical contractor, staying the same whatever the number of jobs?
options: The cable used on each job
Overtime paid in a busy week
Monthly rent for the workshop
Fuel used driving to each site

questions.stem: How can a crew best keep track of its KPI results week by week?
options: A KPI chart updated on the workshop wall
A note kept in the manager's private diary
A spoken update given once a year
The supplier's monthly statement

questions.stem: 17 of 20 new installations passed the government electrical inspection first time. What is the first-time pass rate?
A crew had 6 callbacks from 120 completed jobs this quarter. What is its callback rate?
A crew installed 90 light points in 36 working hours. What was its rate of work?
options: 3 points per hour
4 points per hour
0.4 points per hour
2.5 points per hour

questions.stem: The first-time inspection pass rate has fallen for two months in a row. What is the best next step?
options: Look at the failure reasons and find the common cause
Stop booking inspections until the rate improves
Change the KPI target so the rate looks better
Warn every electrician that their pay will be cut next month

questions.stem: Which is a likely risk to an electrical contractor's operational plan in Jamaica between June and November?
options: Too many trainees asking for work placements
Clients paying all their bills too early
Hurricanes delaying sites and deliveries
The cost of paper for job sheets going up

questions.stem: Copper cable has been stolen from two building sites. Which control fits best in the plan?
options: Leave cable on site overnight to save time
Deliver cable just in time and lock it away
Stop using copper cable on any of the jobs

questions.stem: On a 1–5 scale, a risk has a likelihood of 4 and a consequence of 5. Using likelihood × consequence, what is its score?
Your only electrician trained in fire alarm systems may be away during a big fire alarm job. Which contingency is best?
options: Hope that he does not fall sick that month
Ask the client to delay the job if it happens
Let an untrained worker do it if he is away
Train a second person beforehand

questions.stem: The plan includes new solar PV work, but nobody on the crew has done it before. What should the supervisor do?
options: Let the crew learn by trying it on the client's roof
Arrange approved training before the work starts
Refuse every solar job that the company is offered
Tell the client that the crew is already experienced

questions.stem: A new electrician starts on Monday. What should happen on his first day?
options: Send him straight to work on a live board alone
Give him the van keys and the week's job list
An induction on safety, rules, people and his role
Ask him to read through the company's accounts

questions.stem: Two crew members will be on leave in the same busy week. When should this be dealt with?
options: On the Monday of that week, once they have gone
After the jobs run late and the client complains
At the planning stage, using the leave roster
Never; the others must just work faster

questions.stem: A client moves the date of a job, and this changes the crew's weekly plan. Who must be told?
options: Everyone affected: the crew, stores and manager
Only the stores, so that the materials can be moved in time
Nobody, as the crew will find out on the day
Only the client's own office staff

questions.stem: Which item belongs in a weekly progress report on the plan?
options: News about other contractors' crews
The crew's personal phone numbers
The football results from the weekend
Jobs done against plan, issues and actions

questions.stem: Why should a report on a missed KPI include the cause and a proposed action?
options: So the report is longer and looks more serious
So managers can decide on the fix quickly
So the blame can be put on one person
So the KPI can be taken out of the plan

questions.stem: Job sheets show the hours, materials and test results for each job. Why must they be filled in fully every day?
options: They give the true data used to monitor the plan
They are only needed if a client complains
They replace the need for any separate test certificate
They are used to decide holiday dates

questions.stem: The crew's test results and client details are kept on a shared office computer. How should they be protected?
options: Left open so anyone in the office can edit them
Copied onto personal phones for easy access
Printed and pinned on the workshop notice board
Password-protected, for those who need them

questions.stem: Which change would most reduce the time crews waste travelling between jobs?
options: Give each crew a faster van
Start every job an hour earlier
Group each day's jobs by area of the parish
Let crews choose their own jobs each morning

questions.stem: Inspection failures are often caused by missing labels and missing test certificates. Which change to the plan helps most?
options: Book the inspections later in the month
Add a handover checklist signed by the lead
Use a different inspector each time
Take the pass rate out of the KPIs

questions.stem: To save time, the draft plan has a trainee testing alone at a live board. What should you do?
options: Accept it, as the plan has already been printed
Raise it and change the plan to safe, supervised work
Let the trainee do it only when the job is late
Ask the trainee whether he feels confident enough

questions.stem: A client asks you to leave out the RCD on a circuit to save money, but the specification requires it. What should you do?
options: Explain why it is needed and keep to the specification
Leave it out, as the client is the one who is paying for it
Fit the RCD but leave it unconnected
Leave it out and record that it was fitted

questions.stem: On the same morning, a clinic reports a power failure in a treatment room and a shop wants new display lights fitted. What should decide the order?
options: Which client pays the higher rate
Which job is closer to the workshop
Which job the crew would prefer to do
Safety risk, urgency and contract terms

questions.stem: Which planning tool shows each crew's jobs across the weeks of the plan?
options: A pie chart of last year's costs
A list of the crew's phone numbers
A Gantt chart or job schedule
The supplier's product catalogue

questions.stem: At the end of the plan period, why hold a review of what went well and what went badly?
options: So the lessons are used in the next plan
So the results can be kept secret
So poor results can be blamed on the weather
So the plan never needs writing again

questions.stem: A job needs J$600,000 of switchgear bought now, but the client pays 60 days after completion. What should the plan arrange?
options: Nothing, since the client will pay in the end
Buy cheaper switchgear to save the money
Pay the supplier only when the client pays
A deposit or stage payments to cover cash flow

questions.stem: One of the crew vans will be off the road for a week for repairs. What is the best first step?
options: Cancel all of that crew's jobs for the week
Check the schedule and arrange cover or re-plan
Use a crew member's own car without asking
Leave the problem until the van is back

questions.stem: Halfway through the month, the crew has completed 40% of the planned jobs. What does this suggest?
options: The crew is well ahead of the plan
The plan is running exactly on schedule
The crew is behind and may need help
The month's work is already complete

questions.stem: A colleague asks you to sign test results for a job you did not see tested, so that a KPI date is met. What should you do?
options: Refuse, and report that the tests are not done
Sign it, as meeting the KPI date matters more than anything
Sign it now and test it some time next week
Copy the results from a similar job instead

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the time called when a crew is paid but cannot work, for example while it waits for late materials?
What one word names the planned amount of money set for each cost heading over a period?
Transport was budgeted at J$400,000 for the quarter and cost J$436,000. Give the overspend as a percentage of the budget.
The materials budget is J$75,000 a month. What is the budget for a full year, in J$?
What name is given to a cost that rises and falls with the amount of work done, such as the cable used?
What is the record called that lists each change made to the plan, with the date, the reason and who approved it?
A crew completed 38 of its 40 planned jobs this month. What percentage did it complete?
Which document lists each risk to the plan with its likelihood, consequence, rating, control and owner?
What four-letter name is given to an analysis of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats?
What one word names the money coming in from jobs done, before any costs are taken off?
A job is estimated at 3 electricians working for 5 days of 8 hours each. How many labour hours is that?
An electrical contractor adds a sales tax to its quotations at the current rate. What three letters name this Jamaican tax?
A cost comes in under budget. Is this a favourable or an adverse variance?
What is the name for a planned point that marks the end of a key stage of a job, such as 'rough-in complete'?
What word names the measure of how much useful work is produced for each hour worked?

essays.stem: Your company wins a contract to wire 12 houses in a St Catherine housing scheme over three months, on top of its normal maintenance work. Each house needs about 80 labour hours. Explain how you would help work out the resources needed for the plan. Include the labour calculation.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would work out the labour. Twelve houses at 80 hours each need 12 × 80 = 960 labour hours, or 320 hours a month over three months. I would add the hours the maintenance contracts already use, from past job sheets, and compare the total with the hours the crew has available after leave, training and public holidays. If there is a gap, I would suggest ways to close it, such as approved overtime, a temporary electrician or moving some maintenance visits. Next I would list the materials from the drawings for one house, such as cable, boxes, breakers, panels and outlets, and multiply by twelve, with a small allowance for waste, so the stores can order in good time. I would check the vans, tools, ladders and test instruments, including calibration dates, and book any extra equipment. I would put the resource needs and their costs in J$ into a table and give it to the manager for the budget.
markingPoints: Calculates 960 hours (about 320 hours a month)
Adds existing work and compares with hours available
Suggests realistic ways to close any gap
Lists materials from the drawings, with an allowance for waste
Checks vans, tools and calibrated testers, and costs the resources

essays.stem: Explain how an operational plan links to a company's strategic (business) plan, and how a lead electrician can contribute to preparing it.
essays.modelAnswer: The strategic plan sets the company's long-term direction, for example to double its maintenance contracts in three years. The operational plan is the short-term plan, often for a year or less, that turns that direction into action: the jobs, targets, people, equipment, materials, budget, timeline and risks for each team. Without it, the strategic goals stay as words. A lead electrician knows the work on the ground, so he can give useful input. He can say how long typical jobs really take, using job sheets, and which tools, vans and testers the crew needs. He can point out risks, such as skills gaps, old equipment or supplier delays, and suggest improvements, such as better van stock or grouping jobs by area. He can collect his crew's ideas and concerns and pass them on. Once the plan is agreed, he explains it to the crew, leads them to meet the targets and reports progress.
markingPoints: Describes the strategic plan as long-term direction
Describes the operational plan as short-term action with resources and targets
Explains how one carries out the other
Gives examples of a lead electrician's input
Explains the lead's part in communicating and delivering the plan

essays.stem: Suggest four KPIs for an electrical contracting crew. For each, give a sensible target, say where the data comes from, and explain why it matters.
essays.modelAnswer: First-time inspection pass rate, with a target such as 95% each quarter. The data comes from inspection results on the job files. It matters because failures cost time and money and upset clients. Callback rate, such as below 3% of completed jobs each quarter, from the job log of returns to fix faults. Callbacks show poor workmanship and cost free labour. Jobs finished by the agreed date, such as 90% each month, from the job schedule and completion dates. It shows whether planning and resources are working, and keeps clients happy. Lost-time injuries, with a target of zero, from the accident and near-miss register. Safety comes first, and injuries harm people and stop work. Each KPI needs clear data collected the same way every time, a time period, and a named person to report it. I would show the KPIs on a chart with a target line at the crew's weekly meeting, so that problems are seen early.
markingPoints: Gives four suitable KPIs for electrical work
Each has a realistic, measurable target and time period
States the data source for each
Explains why each matters
Explains how the KPIs are collected, shown and used

essays.stem: For one month, labour was budgeted at J$800,000 and cost J$880,000; materials were budgeted at J$1,200,000 and cost J$1,140,000; transport was budgeted at J$150,000 and cost J$165,000. Work out each variance in J$ and as a percentage, and the total. Then explain what the supervisor should do.
essays.modelAnswer: Labour: J$880,000 − J$800,000 = J$80,000 over budget, which is 80,000 ÷ 800,000 = 10% over (adverse). Materials: J$1,140,000 − J$1,200,000 = J$60,000 under budget, which is 60,000 ÷ 1,200,000 = 5% under (favourable). Transport: J$165,000 − J$150,000 = J$15,000 over, which is 10% over (adverse). The total budget was J$2,150,000 and the total actual was J$2,185,000, so the month was J$35,000 over budget, about 1.6%. The supervisor should look for the causes. Labour may be over because of overtime, jobs taking longer than estimated or rework. Transport may be over because of extra trips or higher fuel prices. Materials being under may be good, or may mean some materials are not yet billed or jobs are behind, so it should be checked. The supervisor should report the figures with the causes and suggest actions, such as better job planning, grouping jobs by area to cut travel, and checking estimates against job sheets.
markingPoints: Labour J$80,000 or 10% over
Materials J$60,000 or 5% under
Transport J$15,000 or 10% over, and total J$35,000 (about 1.6%) over
Suggests likely causes, including checking the favourable variance
Reports with causes and proposes corrective actions

essays.stem: Describe how an electrical contractor in Jamaica should plan for the hurricane season in its operational plan.
essays.modelAnswer: The plan should list the risks the season brings: storms stopping work on site, damage to partly finished installations, flooding of the workshop or stores, power and phone outages, delayed deliveries from ports and suppliers, staff unable to travel, and a rush of urgent repair calls afterwards. Each risk is rated for likelihood and consequence and given controls. Before the season, the company can schedule outdoor and roof work earlier, keep extra stock of common items, raise stores off the floor and make sure vans are fuelled and serviced. During a warning, crews make sites safe: isolate temporary supplies, secure materials and ladders, and protect open panels. Records and backups should be stored safely. After a storm, the plan should say how to check sites safely, how to treat flooded equipment, which clients get priority, such as clinics and water pumps, and how to handle extra overtime. Everyone should know the contact plan. The risk register is reviewed each year after the season.
markingPoints: Identifies several realistic hurricane-season risks
Rates the risks and sets controls
Preparation before the season: scheduling, stock, stores and vans
Actions during a warning to make sites safe
Recovery plan with priorities, safe checks and review

essays.stem: A major client asks for a large job to be brought forward by two weeks. Explain how you would help re-plan the crew's work and keep the rest of the plan on track.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first get the details in writing: the new dates, the scope and any penalty or bonus. Then I would look at the crew's schedule to see which jobs clash and how many labour hours the job needs in the new period. I would check whether the materials and equipment can arrive in time, especially items with long delivery times, such as panels and switchgear. Next I would work out options: moving less urgent jobs later with those clients' agreement, approved overtime, a temporary electrician or splitting the crew. I would cost each option in J$ and check the effect on safety and quality, because rushing must not mean skipped tests or tired workers. I would present the options to the manager for a decision. Once agreed, I would update the schedule and change log, tell everyone affected, including the stores and the other clients, and watch the KPIs closely in the following weeks to see whether the rest of the plan stays on track.
markingPoints: Confirms the change details in writing
Checks clashes, labour hours and material lead times
Develops and costs realistic options
Protects safety and quality
Gets a decision, updates the plan, communicates and monitors

essays.stem: The operational plan includes solar PV installations, but the crew has no experience of them. Explain how a supervisor can support getting the right skills in place.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would compare the skills the solar work needs, such as DC wiring, roof work, inverter connection and testing, with the skills the crew has now. This shows the gap. I would talk to the manager about the options: training some of the current crew through an approved course, hiring an experienced solar electrician, or using a specialist subcontractor for the first jobs while our crew learns alongside. I would plan the training in time for the start of the work and include safety topics, such as working at height and the fact that panels produce voltage whenever light falls on them. For a new hire, I would help write the job description, sit in on interviews if asked, and give a full induction. On the first jobs, I would pair trained and new workers and check their work closely. I would record each person's training and update the plan's resources if the training takes people away from other jobs.
markingPoints: Identifies the skills gap by comparing needs with current skills
Considers training, recruitment and subcontracting
Times the training before the work and includes safety
Supports recruitment and induction
Supervises early jobs and records training, updating the plan

essays.stem: Describe how you would monitor your crew's progress against the operational plan each week, and what you would do when a result falls short.
essays.modelAnswer: I would make sure the crew fills in job sheets every day with hours, materials, test results and any problems, as these give the data. Each week I would compare the actual results with the plan: jobs finished against the schedule, hours against estimates, spending against the budget and the KPIs, such as first-time pass rate and callbacks. I would show the results on a KPI board or chart with the target lines, and go through them at a short weekly crew meeting, so everyone sees how we are doing. When a result falls short, I would look for the cause, not someone to blame, using the job sheets and by asking the crew. For example, slow progress may come from waiting for materials or from rework. I would agree a corrective action with a person and a date, and if the action is outside my authority, such as extra staff, I would report it to the manager with the figures. I would check the next week whether the action worked.
markingPoints: Uses daily job sheets as the data source
Compares actual results with schedule, hours, budget and KPIs weekly
Shows results visibly and discusses them with the crew
Finds the cause of a shortfall and agrees an action, owner and date
Reports beyond their authority and checks the action worked

essays.stem: The crew is behind schedule, and some members want to skip the final tests on jobs to catch up. Explain how you would respond and why.
essays.modelAnswer: I would not allow the tests to be skipped. Testing proves that an installation is safe: that the earth path is sound, the insulation is good, polarity is correct and the protective devices will work. Without it, a fault could cause a fire or a fatal shock, and the company could face legal action, lose its good name and fail the government inspection. Signing a certificate for tests not done is dishonest and may be against the law. I would explain this calmly to the crew and remind them that the plan's targets never come before safety and quality. Then I would deal with the real problem, which is the delay. I would look at why the crew is behind, such as late materials or too many jobs, and report it to the manager with options: re-planning dates with clients, approved overtime or extra help. I would record the decision and keep the KPI figures honest, as false results hide the problem and stop it being fixed.
markingPoints: Refuses to allow the tests to be skipped
Explains the safety purpose of testing
Explains legal, inspection and reputation consequences and honesty
Finds the cause of the delay and proposes real solutions
Reports to the manager and keeps records honest

essays.stem: At the end of a six-month plan period, explain how you would help review the plan and use the results to improve the next plan.
essays.modelAnswer: I would gather the facts first: the KPI results against their targets, the budget against actual spending, jobs completed against the schedule, and the risk register showing which risks happened. I would also collect the crew's views on what helped and what got in the way, and any client feedback. With the manager, I would compare the results with the objectives and pick out what went well, such as a fall in callbacks after the handover checklist, and what went badly, such as labour overruns on commercial jobs. For each shortfall I would look for the cause, such as estimates that were too low or delays from one supplier. Then I would suggest changes for the next plan: better estimates based on real job sheet hours, new or changed KPIs, extra training, a second supplier, or different stock levels. I would write the findings in a short review report, share them with the crew, and keep the report so the lessons are not lost.
markingPoints: Gathers results on KPIs, budget, schedule and risks
Collects crew and client feedback
Identifies what went well and badly, with causes
Proposes specific improvements for the next plan
Records the review and shares it with the crew

practical1.title: Prepare the resource, budget and risk sections of a quarter's operational plan for an electrical crew
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a planning pack for an electrical contractor's crew for the next three months: a list of jobs with estimated labour hours (for example, wiring houses in a housing scheme, a shop fit-out and a hotel maintenance contract), the crew list with leave dates, the vans and test instruments with their calibration dates, a materials list with J$ prices, and the GCT rate to use. As a group, prepare the plan sections on the forms provided. Share the roles: one member writes three SMART objectives and four KPIs with targets; one makes the labour table (hours needed per month compared with hours available after leave, with the gap and how to close it); one makes the equipment and vehicle schedule, including calibration bookings and spares; one prepares the materials and cost budget by month, adding GCT at the rate given; and one writes a risk register with at least five risks, each rated with controls and an owner. The group checks every calculation together. Finally, present the plan to the assessor, playing the operations manager, in ten minutes, with every member presenting their section. Photograph each stage below.
materials: Planning pack: job list with hours, crew list and leave dates, equipment list, materials prices and the GCT rate (supplied by the assessor)
Blank objectives and KPI, labour, equipment, budget and risk register forms
Calculators, or a computer with a spreadsheet
photos: The SMART objectives and KPI table
The labour table showing the gap and how it will be closed
The equipment and vehicle schedule with calibration dates
The monthly materials and cost budget with GCT
The presentation, with each member speaking
checklist: Wrote objectives that are specific, measurable and time-bound
Calculated labour hours, gaps and costs correctly
Scheduled calibration and spares so work is not stopped
Prepared a budget that adds up and applies GCT correctly
Identified realistic risks with suitable controls and owners
Presented their section clearly and answered questions
safety: This is a desk task: no electrical work is done
Plans must never schedule live work or unsupervised trainees
Use only the made-up data in the pack; do not use real client or staff details
Share the workload fairly and respect each other's ideas

practical2.title: Run a weekly KPI review and re-plan after a change (role play)
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group the operational plan for an electrical crew and the results for week 6: jobs finished, hours worked, inspection results, callbacks, spending and incidents. Then the assessor gives a change card, for example 'a key electrician is off sick for two weeks, the breaker supplier is three weeks late, and a hotel client wants its job brought forward'. As a group, first update a KPI board poster: work out each KPI and draw it on a chart against its target line. Next, re-plan: update the job schedule (Gantt chart) for the next four weeks, list the options for each problem with their cost in J$ and effect on the plan, and agree the best option. Write a one-page change log and action list with owners and dates. Then hold a role-played weekly review meeting: one member chairs as the lead electrician, one presents the KPI board, one presents the revised schedule, one plays the operations manager using the assessor's role card and asks hard questions, and one takes the minutes. Swap the presenter roles once, so every member speaks. Photograph each stage below.
materials: Operational plan extract and week 6 results (supplied by the assessor)
Change card and manager's role card (supplied by the assessor)
Poster paper, graph paper, rulers and coloured markers
Blank Gantt chart, change log, action list and minutes forms
photos: The KPI board poster with charts and target lines
The options list with costs and the chosen option
The review meeting, at each change of presenter
The change log, action list and minutes
checklist: Calculated the KPIs correctly from the results
Drew clear charts with target lines
Compared options with costs and effect on safety and quality
Set actions with owners and dates
Spoke clearly in the meeting and answered the manager's questions
Kept accurate minutes or checked them
safety: This is a desk and role-play task: no electrical work is done
No option may cut testing, safe isolation or supervision to save time
Keep any staff illness details in the scenario private and respectful
Disagree politely in the meeting; no personal remarks
